title: Branching & Merging
description: Work on features independently and merge changes safely

comicStory.title: The Parallel Universe Developer

panels.text: Meet Alex, working on a website. Boss says: 'Add login feature, but don't break the live site!'
Without branches: Alex edits main code directly. Half-done login breaks everything. Site crashes! 💥
With branches: Alex creates 'feature-login' branch. Works in parallel universe! Main site stays safe.
Alex completes login feature in branch. Tests it. Everything works perfectly!
TWIST: Alex merges branch into main. But teammate also changed same file! Merge conflict! 😱
Alex resolves conflict, merges successfully. Login feature live! Main site never broke during development!

comicStory.twist: Branches let you work safely in parallel, but merging requires handling conflicts!
comicStory.lesson: Branching = Parallel development. Merging = Combining work. Conflicts = Manual resolution needed!

deepDive.whatItIs: Branching creates separate lines of development where you can work independently without affecting the main codebase. Merging combines changes from different branches back together. Think of branches as parallel universes where you can experiment safely.
deepDive.whyItMatters: Without branching, all developers would work on the same code simultaneously, causing chaos and breaking the main codebase. Branches enable safe experimentation, parallel development, and organized collaboration. They're essential for team workflows and feature development.
whereUsed: Feature Development: Create branch for each new feature
Bug Fixes: Isolate bug fixes in separate branches
Team Collaboration: Multiple developers work on different branches
Release Management: Maintain separate branches for different versions
Experimentation: Try new ideas without risk

visualExamples.diagram:
Fast-Forward (no new commits on main):

               \

After merge:
main:     A --- B --- C --- D

               \
feature:        C --- D

interactiveQA.question: What is a branch in Git?
interactiveQA.answer: A separate line of development where you can work independently without affecting the main codebase.
interactiveQA.explanation: Branch is like a parallel universe. You can make changes, experiment, and develop features without touching the main code. Once ready, you merge it back.

interactiveQA.question: Why use branches?
interactiveQA.answer: To develop features, fix bugs, and collaborate safely without breaking the main code.
interactiveQA.explanation: Branches allow: safe experimentation, parallel development, isolated bug fixes, team collaboration, and keeping main code stable. Essential for professional development!

interactiveQA.question: How to create a new branch?
interactiveQA.answer: Use 'git branch branch-name' to create, then 'git checkout branch-name' to switch to it.
interactiveQA.explanation: git branch creates the branch. git checkout switches to it. Shortcut: git checkout -b branch-name (creates and switches in one command).

interactiveQA.question: What does 'git merge' do?
interactiveQA.answer: Combines changes from one branch into another (usually into main).
interactiveQA.explanation: Merging integrates work from feature branch into main branch. First checkout main, then git merge feature-branch. This brings all feature changes into main.

interactiveQA.question: What is a merge conflict?
interactiveQA.answer: When two branches modify the same part of code differently, requiring manual resolution.
interactiveQA.explanation: Conflict occurs when Git can't automatically merge because same lines were changed differently. You must manually choose which changes to keep.

interactiveQA.question: What is fast-forward merge?
interactiveQA.answer: When no new commits exist on main, Git simply moves forward and adds branch commits.
interactiveQA.explanation: If main hasn't changed since branch was created, Git just moves main pointer forward to include branch commits. No merge commit needed. Simple and clean!

codingChallenge.title: Branch and Merge Workflow
codingChallenge.scenario: You're working on a project. Create a feature branch, make changes, and merge it back to main. Simulate the complete branching workflow.
codingChallenge.problem: Simulate Git branching: create branch, add commits, merge to main, and handle the workflow.
codingChallenge.expectedOutput:
Created branch: feature-login
Committed: Add login form
Committed: Add validation
Merged feature-login into main
Main now has 3 commits
hints: Create a Branch class to represent branches
Implement merge() to combine branch commits into main
codingChallenge.solution:
class GitBranching:
    def __init__(self):
        self.branches = {'main': []}
        self.current_branch = 'main'
    
    def create_branch(self, name):
        # Copy current branch commits to new branch
        self.branches[name] = self.branches[self.current_branch].copy()
        print(f"Created branch: {name}")
    
    def checkout(self, name):
        if name in self.branches:
            self.current_branch = name
            print(f"Switched to branch: {name}")
        else:
            print(f"Branch {name} does not exist")
    
    def commit(self, message):
        self.branches[self.current_branch].append(message)
        print(f"Committed: {message}")
    
    def merge(self, branch_name):
        if branch_name not in self.branches:
            print(f"Branch {branch_name} does not exist")
            return
        
        # Get commits from branch that aren't in current branch
        branch_commits = self.branches[branch_name]
        current_commits = self.branches[self.current_branch]
        
        # Add new commits from branch
        for commit in branch_commits:
            if commit not in current_commits:
                current_commits.append(commit)
        
        print(f"Merged {branch_name} into {self.current_branch}")
    
    def log(self):
        commits = self.branches[self.current_branch]
        print(f"{self.current_branch} now has {len(commits)} commits")
        for commit in commits:
            print(f"  - {commit}")

# Usage
git = GitBranching()

# Initial commit on main
git.commit("Initial commit")

# Create and switch to feature branch
git.create_branch("feature-login")
git.checkout("feature-login")

# Work on feature
git.commit("Add login form")
git.commit("Add validation")

# Switch back to main and merge
git.checkout("main")
git.merge("feature-login")
git.log()
codingChallenge.explanation: This simulates Git branching: create_branch() creates new branch, checkout() switches branches, commit() adds commits to current branch, merge() combines branch commits into current branch. In real Git: git branch, git checkout, git commit, git merge.

quiz.question: What is a branch in Git?
quiz.explanation: A branch is a separate line of development where you can work independently without affecting other branches. It's like a parallel version of your code.

quiz.question: Why use branches?
options: To work on features safely without breaking main code
quiz.explanation: Branches allow safe parallel development. You can work on features, fix bugs, and experiment without affecting the main codebase. Essential for team collaboration!

quiz.question: How to create a new branch?
quiz.explanation: git branch branch-name creates a new branch. To switch to it, use git checkout branch-name. Shortcut: git checkout -b branch-name (creates and switches).

quiz.question: How to switch to a different branch?
options: git checkout branch-name or git switch branch-name
quiz.explanation: git checkout branch-name switches to the branch. Newer syntax: git switch branch-name. Both work the same way.

quiz.question: What does 'git merge' do?
options: Combines changes from one branch into another
quiz.explanation: git merge combines changes from one branch into your current branch. Usually used to merge feature branches into main. First checkout main, then git merge feature-branch.

quiz.question: What is a merge conflict?
options: When two branches modify the same code differently
quiz.explanation: Merge conflict occurs when two branches change the same lines of code differently. Git can't automatically decide which to keep, so you must manually resolve it.

quiz.question: What is fast-forward merge?
options: When main hasn't changed, Git moves pointer forward
quiz.explanation: Fast-forward merge happens when main branch hasn't changed since feature branch was created. Git simply moves main pointer forward to include feature commits. No merge commit needed!

quiz.question: Best practice before merging?
options: Pull latest changes from main and test your branch
quiz.explanation: Before merging: 1) Pull latest main changes, 2) Merge main into your branch, 3) Test everything works, 4) Then merge your branch into main. Prevents conflicts and bugs!

quiz.question: How to delete a branch after merging?
quiz.explanation: git branch -d branch-name deletes a branch after it's been merged. Use -D (capital D) to force delete unmerged branch. Good practice to clean up merged branches!
